DATA MUST FALL

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
South African Data Costs are exorbitant - we rank the 16th most expensive in the Africa - restricting access to the internet can severely impede the overall economic and social progress of a country. #DataMustFall is a campaign that affects every single South African.

Summary:
The #DataMustFall campaign started last week when the radio personality known as Tbo Touch started the hashtag on Twitter, drawing attention to the sometimes astronomical costs of wireless data in a country where the majority of people access the internet via mobile phones.

When radio DJ Thabo Molefe tweeted his anger at South Africa’s unreasonably high cellular data costs, he didn’t know it would lead to a public outcry that would result in two days of parliamentary hearings and intense scrutiny.


Further information:
DATA MUST FALL
The #DataMustFall campaign started last week when the radio personality known as Tbo Touch started the hashtag on Twitter, drawing attention to the sometimes astronomical costs of wireless data in a country where the majority of people access the internet via mobile phones.
When radio DJ Thabo Molefe tweeted his anger at South Africa’s unreasonably high cellular data costs, he didn’t know it would lead to a public outcry that would result in two days of parliamentary hearings and intense scrutiny.
WHO TO INTERVIEW
• DJ THABO MOLEFE (NOT GARETH CLIFF)
• I’ve asked Bron to do a call out for us to find case studies that have been charged crazy amounts out of bundle.
• We’ll do vox pops with a range of South Africans
• We’ll interview Research ICT Africa – they have done extensive research about affordability in Africa and how we compare internationally.
• Then the Alliance for Affordable Internet is an international organization – Onica Makwakwa is the Regional head and has done research into the impact the lack of access to internet has on developing countries.
• AND THEN Government – we’ll try for the Minister or else someone from the Portfolio Committee.
HOW DO WE COMPARE TO OTHER DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
“South Africa’s cheapest 1GB data places it at 16th of out 47 African countries assessed by Research ICT Africa,” the research unit’s executive director Dr Alison Gillwald said in a written submission to parliament. Until recently South Africa had the continent’s largest economy, when it was overtaken by Nigeria and then Egypt, and has the oldest, and most mature, cellphone market.
“Tanzania has the cheapest 1GB for $0.89 in comparison to South Africa priced at $5.26. In comparison to other large markets, Egypt, Kenya and Nigeria have better data prices compared to South Africa. Regionally, data prices remain expensive.”
Research ICT Africa estimates that users in the “lower income category, are spending significant portions of their income, around 20%, on relatively small amounts of data (1GB)”.
The UN recommends 500MB should cost less than 5% of income for all income groups, she said.
EXCLUDING THE POOR
The Alliance for Affordable Internet (A4AI) has done similar research in the field. “For almost half the South African population, a seemingly affordable mobile Internet connection (priced at about 1.5% of ‘average’ monthly income) actually costs anywhere between 7-15% of their income,” according to A4AI, whose 2015-16 Affordability Report covers policy frameworks in 51 emerging countries and how it affects affordable broadband access.
Not being able to access the Internet stagnates development
In an age when many of us take for granted, and increasingly rely on, access to the internet -- whether on our smart phones or in our homes and offices -- it is hard to imagine that two-thirds of the global population is not online.
The benefits of today’s information and communications technologies (ICTs), especially the internet, are not distributed evenly. Two out of three households in developing countries do not have internet access of any kind, compared to just 20 percent of households in developed countries. Of the two billion people in the developing world who have some internet access, many are limited to using costly mobile services that lack the quality and utility of high-speed broadband. Thus, many of the world’s poorest people are excluded from the benefits of reliable, affordable connectivity, including access to key tools that support sectors from healthcare to education, as well as entrepreneurs and small businesses. This is especially troublesome when you consider that a 2009 World Bank Report found that a 10 percent increase in broadband penetration can lead to a 1.38 percent increase in GDP growth in developing countries. Simply put, underdeveloped ICT in a country can severely impede overall economic and social progress.
OUT OF BUNDLE EXPLOITATION
While most people buy out data bundles, if that bundle expires people pay ZAR2 ($0,146) per megabyte or an outrageous R2,000 ($146) a gigabyte.
South Africa’s parliamentary Portfolio Committee on Telecommunications and Postal Services heard from the cellular operators today and other interested parties yesterday, including Molefe and his business partner Gareth Cliff, another significant South African radio personality who launched his own streaming radio service, CliffCentral.com, two years ago.
A4AI regional head Onica Makwakwa said income inequality in general also masked the true picture of internet access.
Emphasis should also be on community-owned networks.

Press Release:


#DataMustFall How does the cost of data affect you? Radio DJ Tbo Touch’s #DataMustFall campaign to slash what are said to be exorbitant data charges – among the highest in the world – has gone viral, even reaching parliament. Carte Blanche investigates the cost of staying connected.


Script:


DATA MUST FALL STRUCTURE

VO: The Internet is undoubtedly a powerful tool - citizens of the world connect, communicate and share information – but it’s power, is not shared by everyone - the cost to communicate denies billions of people access.

DJ TOUCH: this is what the world is today – analog age is stone age – if info is expensive to access – why do we position ourselves to be developed nation.

VO: Radio Personality Thabo Molefe, popularly known as DJ Tbo TOUCH, streams his radio show online.

UPSOUND RADIO

VO: Frustrated with the high cost of mobile data in South Africa, he took to social media starting the DataMustFall movement.

VOXPOPS
MBUSO: I’m plus minus spending about R600 just on data
NAOMI: I would pay like R1500 in a month or even R2000

DJ TOUCH: Support from society – ventersdorp to Stellenbosch – as been amazing – we are not at war with networks – but if you got something to hide – then you will see this campaign as provocative.

LINK: The campaign gained momentum – and went viral - within a week it had made it to parliament.

KUBAYI: When there is a voice rising can’t fold your arms and be passive and not respond to it.

VO: The Portfolio Committee on Telecommunications held public hearings on the impact of high mobile data costs in information and communications technology or ICT chaired by Mmamoloko Kubayi.

KUBAYI: cost to communication is very important// ICT is the back bone of the economy

VO: Research ICT Africa found that South Africa ranks 16th out of 47 on the African affordability list, comparing the cheapest rates for 1GB of mobile data – that’s behind Tanzania, Mozambique and Ghana.

Onica Makwakwa is from the Alliance for Affordable Internet – the world’s broadest technology sector coalition.

ONICA: We are 7 to 10 times more expensive than other African countries who are basically our peers or smaller economies.
KUBAYI: Taking countries

FARHANNA: It upsets me – why is our data more?

VO: Farhanna Khan has a household of 6 – data not a luxury for them.

FARHANNA: It is an essential – we have kids, especially when they come from school – we do have to put it in our budget.

LINK: In a world that is all about connectivity – data in not just a luxury but an absolute necessity – without it people are literally cut off from information, development, and progress.

VO: In fact, the United Nations proclaimed access to Internet as a basic human right in July this year.

ONICA: Access to the internet and affordability is really an issue of global competitiveness in terms of youth, employment and education –

VO: In South Africa, 14.9 million households have access to mobile phones but only 6 million of those have access to the Internet using mobile data – the biggest driving factor, is affordability.

21 year old Naomi Matthews uses it socially and professionally.

NAOMI: Times have changed – the only way of communicating is through technology

VO: 25 year old Mbuso Zondo says he goes out of bundle every month.

MBUSO: It’s ridiculous – something needs to be done we should be paying a lot less…

VO: Of the four major mobile operators – Vodacom & MTN responded in writing, while smaller challenger networks that don’t operate in Africa - Telkom and Cell C - spoke to us on camera.

Cell C’s Graham MacKinnon says they are listening to consumer needs, and offer some of the cheapest mobile data in the market.

BONGANI: Cheaper in SA – but not comparitively
GRAHAM: Yes – some structural issues in the SA telecommunication market unfortunately people compete on infrastructure – should be competing on service

DJ TOUCH: We have been ripped off for years. And we are saying be mindful – it’s a R160 for 1Gb brutal

VO: MTN & Vodacom blame cost drivers which differ from country to country. Aside from geographical size and population density - Vodacom refers to “… taxes, spectrum license fees, import duties and rental fees for undersea cables…”. While MTN add the impact of “electricity tariffs, fuel prices and handset prices that are denominated in foreign currency.”

Input costs in South Africa affect all networks, says Telkom’s Jacqui O’Sullivan.

JACQUI: The input costs in a tough economic climate are difficult, //we certainly do need to look at the sub one gig spectrum and how the regulator wishes to allocate it is absolutely critical in furthering the accessibility of high speed broadband.

VO: Spectrum refers to radio frequencies used by mobile operators to reach further into areas, connecting more people at faster speeds with less infrastructure costs.

It’s something all four big mobile network operators have been calling for. But there have been delays from a regulatory and legislative perspective.

KUBAYI: what needs be clear – being let down by ICASA – have to do what is right –age. //We’ve been saying for 8 years – can still grow the sector. Impacting negatively

VO: ICASA proposed auctioning off high speed spectrum licences – a move that was challenged by the Minister of Telecommunications and smaller networks.

ICASA’s Acting Chairman, Rubben Mohlaloga, spoke to us on Wednesday prior to the ruling.

MOHLALOGA: We are in court – if I were to explain may run the risk of dealing sub judice INT1 M8// as the authority we are trying to address the constraints hampering the growth of high speed broadband and fast internet.

VO: On Friday the High Court granted the interdict preventing ICASA from auctioning off these licenses – now the allocation process will be reviewed.

With the hearings concluded, Kubayi and her team will compile legislative and regulatory recommendations in a report.

BONGANI – profitable – gonna change.
KUBAYI: We want business to thrive // remember they contribute to GDP // must happen responsibly and reasonably // not at the expense of poor people // it shouldn’t be out of greed, it shoudn’t be out of arrogance
BONGANI – what if they don’t
KUBAYI: We will have to push them. Maybe sealing off costs.

VO: While all four big networks say they are committed to finding innovative pricing solutions – Tbo Touch says better data is critical for South Africans to feature in global markets.

DJ TOUCH: We don’t want to make free calls between midnight and 5 – we are sleeping at that time – empower me data so I can wake up in the morning to do business.






PROMOS

PROMO 2 – 15 seconds
VO: The DataMustFall campaign highlights the high cost to communicate in South Africa.

ONICA: We are 7 to 10 times more expensive than other African countries

PROMO 3 – 15 seconds
VO: DJ Tbo Touch kickstarted the #datamustfall campaign sparking a national call for a cap on high data costs.

DJ TOUCH: We don’t want to make free calls between midnight and 5 – we are sleeping at that time – empower me data so I can wake up in the morning to do business.

PROMO 1 – 10 seconds
VO: High Mobile Data Costs limit progress & development.

DJ TOUCH: // if info is expensive to access – why do we position ourselves to be developed nation.

metadata.Summary: The #DataMustFall campaign started last week when the radio personality known as Tbo Touch started the hashtag on Twitter, drawing attention to the sometimes astronomical costs of wireless data in a country where the majority of people access the internet via mobile phones. When radio DJ Thabo Molefe tweeted his anger at South Africa’s unreasonably high cellular data costs, he didn’t know it would lead to a public outcry that would result in two days of parliamentary hearings and intense scrutiny.
metadata.Further information: DATA MUST FALL The #DataMustFall campaign started last week when the radio personality known as Tbo Touch started the hashtag on Twitter, drawing attention to the sometimes astronomical costs of wireless data in a country where the majority of people access the internet via mobile phones. When radio DJ Thabo Molefe tweeted his anger at South Africa’s unreasonably high cellular data costs, he didn’t know it would lead to a public outcry that would result in two days of parliamentary hearings and intense scrutiny. WHO TO INTERVIEW • DJ THABO MOLEFE (NOT GARETH CLIFF) • I’ve asked Bron to do a call out for us to find case studies that have been charged crazy amounts out of bundle. • We’ll do vox pops with a range of South Africans • We’ll interview Research ICT Africa – they have done extensive research about affordability in Africa and how we compare internationally. • Then the Alliance for Affordable Internet is an international organization – Onica Makwakwa is the Regional head and has done research into the impact the lack of access to internet has on developing countries. • AND THEN Government – we’ll try for the Minister or else someone from the Portfolio Committee. HOW DO WE COMPARE TO OTHER DEVELOPING COUNTRIES “South Africa’s cheapest 1GB data places it at 16th of out 47 African countries assessed by Research ICT Africa,” the research unit’s executive director Dr Alison Gillwald said in a written submission to parliament. Until recently South Africa had the continent’s largest economy, when it was overtaken by Nigeria and then Egypt, and has the oldest, and most mature, cellphone market. “Tanzania has the cheapest 1GB for $0.89 in comparison to South Africa priced at $5.26. In comparison to other large markets, Egypt, Kenya and Nigeria have better data prices compared to South Africa. Regionally, data prices remain expensive.” Research ICT Africa estimates that users in the “lower income category, are spending significant portions of their income, around 20%, on relatively small amounts of data (1GB)”. The UN recommends 500MB should cost less than 5% of income for all income groups, she said. EXCLUDING THE POOR The Alliance for Affordable Internet (A4AI) has done similar research in the field. “For almost half the South African population, a seemingly affordable mobile Internet connection (priced at about 1.5% of ‘average’ monthly income) actually costs anywhere between 7-15% of their income,” according to A4AI, whose 2015-16 Affordability Report covers policy frameworks in 51 emerging countries and how it affects affordable broadband access. Not being able to access the Internet stagnates development In an age when many of us take for granted, and increasingly rely on, access to the internet -- whether on our smart phones or in our homes and offices -- it is hard to imagine that two-thirds of the global population is not online. The benefits of today’s information and communications technologies (ICTs), especially the internet, are not distributed evenly. Two out of three households in developing countries do not have internet access of any kind, compared to just 20 percent of households in developed countries. Of the two billion people in the developing world who have some internet access, many are limited to using costly mobile services that lack the quality and utility of high-speed broadband. Thus, many of the world’s poorest people are excluded from the benefits of reliable, affordable connectivity, including access to key tools that support sectors from healthcare to education, as well as entrepreneurs and small businesses. This is especially troublesome when you consider that a 2009 World Bank Report found that a 10 percent increase in broadband penetration can lead to a 1.38 percent increase in GDP growth in developing countries. Simply put, underdeveloped ICT in a country can severely impede overall economic and social progress. OUT OF BUNDLE EXPLOITATION While most people buy out data bundles, if that bundle expires people pay ZAR2 ($0,146) per megabyte or an outrageous R2,000 ($146) a gigabyte. South Africa’s parliamentary Portfolio Committee on Telecommunications and Postal Services heard from the cellular operators today and other interested parties yesterday, including Molefe and his business partner Gareth Cliff, another significant South African radio personality who launched his own streaming radio service, CliffCentral.com, two years ago. A4AI regional head Onica Makwakwa said income inequality in general also masked the true picture of internet access. Emphasis should also be on community-owned networks.
